bib.title: Chapter 5: Convolutional Neural Networks (Fundamentals of Deep Learning, chapter)

question: How can neural networks be made tractable and effective for image data, and how are convolutional networks built, trained and visualised?
contributions: Motivates CNNs from the failure of hand-picked features and fully connected nets on images
Defines filters, feature maps, convolutional layer arithmetic and max pooling
Worked TensorFlow (1.x) code for MNIST and CIFAR-10 CNNs, batch norm, preprocessing
Visualisation (filters, t-SNE) and neural style transfer

results.claim: A small CNN (two 5x5 conv + 2x2 max-pool, FC 1024 with dropout 0.5, softmax) reaches 99.4% on MNIST, vs 98.2% for the earlier feed-forward net.
results.setup: MNIST, TensorFlow, Adam, 'several epochs'; conv 32 then 64 filters, FC 1,024

results.claim: CIFAR-10 CNN with batch norm reaches 96.7% accuracy vs 92.3% without.
results.setup: CIFAR-10, 2 conv(5x5, 64) + 2 max-pool + FC 384 + FC 192 + softmax, Adam, random 24x24 crops, BN net uses 10x learning rate and keep_prob=1; epochs and base LR not stated
results.quote: 92.3% accuracy on the CIFAR-10 task without batch normalization and 96.7% accuracy with
results.note: Claim that this matches or exceeds state of the art has dated; text says 'potentially exceeds'.

results.claim: Batch norm cuts minibatches needed to cross 90% accuracy on CIFAR-10 from over 80,000 to about 14,000.
results.setup: Same CIFAR-10 pair of networks; read from training curves (Fig 5-17)
results.quote: with batch normalization, crossing the same

results.claim: AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet error was about 16% vs 26.1% for the runner up; 2011 winner had 25.7%.
results.setup: ImageNet challenge as described by the book (200 classes, ~450,000 training images, five guesses)
results.note: The 200 classes/450,000 images description is the book's and does not match the ILSVRC-2012 classification task (1000 classes, ~1.2M images).

results.claim: Viola-Jones face detector: 91.4% detection rate with 50 false positives on 130 images, 507 faces.
results.setup: Viola and Jones 2001, boosted Haar-like intensity features

results.claim: A fully connected first layer on a 200x200 RGB image needs 120,000 weights per neuron, versus 784 for MNIST.
Conv output size formula: w_out = (w_in - e + 2p)/s + 1; example 5x5x3 input, p=1, two 3x3x3 filters, s=2 gives 3x3x2 output.
results.quote: output volume, which will be of size 3 x 3 x 2

results.claim: VGGNet needs about 90 MB per image on forward pass and over 180 MB with backward pass.
results.setup: VGGNet, Simonyan and Zisserman 2014, memory for activations
results.note: Text says forward 90 MB, forward+backward more than 180 MB; per image.

results.claim: Only two pooling variants are common: non-overlapping e=2,s=2 and overlapping e=3,s=2; pooling output size is (w_in - e)/s + 1.
results.quote: only two major variations of the pooling layer are used

limits: TensorFlow 1.x API (tf.get_variable, tf.nn.dropout keep_prob, per_image_whitening, batch_norm_with_global_normalization) is dated; replaced by Keras/PyTorch layers.
Training details missing: epochs, learning rates, batch size, seeds, hardware for MNIST and CIFAR-10 runs; CIFAR-10 numbers are single runs without variance.
Claim of 96.7% CIFAR-10 matching state of the art is dated; later work far exceeds it.
Architectures covered end at VGGNet; no residual connections, no depthwise or 1x1 conv, no modern normalisation; batch norm explained via internal covariate shift intuition.
ImageNet description (200 classes, 450,000 images) differs from the standard classification task.
Style-transfer and t-SNE sections are illustrative, with no quantitative results.
practices: Keep filters small (3x3 or 5x5); 7x7 only in the first conv layer (p.97).
Use stride 1 and zero padding that preserves height and width (p.97).
Use pooling of e=2,s=2 or e=3,s=2 and keep extent small since pooling is destructive; stack several conv layers before each pool in deeper nets (p.99-100).
Initialise conv weights with stddev sqrt(2/fan_in) and ReLU (p.101).
Use dropout p=0.5 in the FC layer during training and 1 at evaluation (p.103).
Use per-image whitening plus random crop/flip/brightness/contrast/saturation/hue augmentation for natural images (p.103).
Apply batch norm to logits before the nonlinearity, raise the learning rate (10x in CIFAR-10 example), drop dropout/L2 (p.105-108).
Plot cost and validation curves, and inspect first-layer filters to check the network learns edges not noise (p.109-111).
Watch GPU memory when going deep; use larger stride/extent in the first conv layer to cut it (p.100-101).
